title: Reading the text as a whole

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Identify a text’s characteristic features and relate each to its meaning, context and audience; characterise its overall style and prove it through specific language choices.

blocks.heading: Characteristic features
blocks.text: The characteristic features of a text are the features that make it recognisably the kind of text it is: its conventions of form, its structural habits, its recurring language choices. A feature is characteristic when it belongs to the kind rather than the instance — the headline belongs to the article; a particular headline belongs to this one — and the analysis uses the instance to show the kind.

blocks.heading: The opening move
blocks.text: The opening move of an analysis fixes the text’s form, audience, purpose and context in a sentence or two, because every feature discussed later is judged by what it does for them. "This is a charity leaflet for the general giving public, written to persuade during a drought appeal" is one sentence that arms every later point; it ends with the overall effect the text has on its reader. The text analysis task is set with the instruction Analyse, is worth twenty-five marks — five for reading, twenty for analysis — and the reading marks credit a subtle, assured grasp of meaning, context and audience, shown by use rather than retelling.

blocks.heading: Style
blocks.text: A text’s overall style is the manner its choices produce together, and it is characterised in two or three precise words — wry and conversational; urgent and plain; intimate and exact — which are then proved through specific choices. The adjectives are the claim; the choices are the evidence; and a claim about style counts only when specific choices prove it, so no adjective is written down without a quotation waiting to follow it.

blocks.heading: Worked example: the opening done properly
blocks.text: Take this opening, written for the purpose: "Nobody tells you that the hardest part of moving a school is the furniture." The form is a first-person column, the audience is general readers with an interest in schools, the purpose is to entertain as much as inform, and the style is wry and confiding: "Nobody tells you" draws the reader into a shared secret, and the joke puts the difficulty in the furniture rather than the children. Two or three precise words, proved at once — the analysis has begun, and the retelling has not started.

blocks.heading: What sits on the reading marks
blocks.text: The reading column of the task’s table credits a subtle, assured grasp of the text’s meaning, context and audience, and it is worth five of the twenty-five marks — a fifth of the task earned or lost in the first two minutes. The grasp is shown by use: an analysis that fixes the frame correctly and then quotes aptly has demonstrated its reading without a single retold event, and an analysis that retells has demonstrated the opposite. Learn the opening move until it is reflex, and the reading marks follow the analysis around like a shadow that has been paid for. The remaining twenty are for what this unit’s companions teach: the style characterisation, the three grounds, the four moves, the organisation and the register.

blocks.heading: Answering the wrong question
blocks.text: The error is responding to the topic of the text: agreeing with its argument, explaining its subject further, or giving an opinion on the matter. Analysis is about how the text is written, and the test is the transplant — if a sentence of the answer would still make sense in an essay about the subject, it is about the topic and not the text. "Fog harvesting is a brilliant idea" is an opinion; "the writer personifies the fog as a visitor to make the reader welcome the scheme" is analysis.
